gist: A third of young British adults have never had sex, according to a major study.
Adults in Great Britain are having sex less frequently than in past decades.
Online sexual activities like sexting and watching pornography have become widespread among young people.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles found British adults are having less sex. Under-45s average sex twice a month, down from four times in 1990. A third of under-25s have never had sex, up from under a fifth in 2010. Meanwhile, half of 16- to 24-year-olds have sent or received sexual images in the past year.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Fewer young women want children, with the proportion doubling to 17% over the past decade. Researchers cite potential factors like economic insecurity, mental health issues, less physical socialising, and living with parents longer. Furthermore, many people still engage in unprotected sex, putting them at risk of sexually transmitted infections and unplanned pregnancies.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Researchers plan to investigate what is driving changing family plans and potential future impacts of AI companions on sexual behaviour. Public health services may also need to adapt to ensure equitable HPV vaccination coverage across all groups.

fivew: Researchers from institutions including UCL and LSHTM surveyed British adults.
A major study found British adults are having less sex while online sexual behaviours have increased.
The survey fieldwork took place between September 2022 and January 2024.
The survey covered people across Great Britain.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The US Army scheduled a controlled explosion of 68 barrels of unstable lead azide at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. The detonation followed several delays caused by public outcry, legal actions from environmental groups, and intervention by Donald Trump. Outlets reported the scheduled time as 10:00 EST and 9:00 CST.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Lead azide is an explosive compound that has crystallised and degraded over decades, creating a risk of spontaneous detonation. A controlled blast aims to limit toxic lead dust, which could travel up to 100 miles and potentially affect hundreds of nearby farms, local communities and water supplies.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Officials recommend that residents within five miles evacuate, while those within 20 miles should stay indoors. The military is using water walls, foam, and gel blocks to contain dust. Further environmental and health testing has been urged.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A US grand jury in Los Angeles has charged 82-year-old Thomas Markle with two counts of possessing child sexual abuse material. FBI officers detained Markle at a Florida care home after searching a storage space he rented in California. Prosecutors allege that agents uncovered 35mm film negatives depicting young children in various stages of undress, alongside photos showing Markle with minors. Markle, who denies the allegations, was initially granted bail in Tampa but was later imprisoned after reportedly tampering with his electronic tracking tag.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Markle is the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex. If convicted on both federal charges, he could receive a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison per count.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: After a judge in Florida ruled Markle mentally fit to face trial, he is expected to appear for arraignment in Los Angeles over the coming weeks.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Sales of motorised quadricycles, or micro-cars, have increased significantly across Europe over the last five years. These vehicles, which do not require a standard driving licence, are increasingly popular with teenagers and older people in rural areas. The launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 helped shift the market, attracting younger buyers who previously used mopeds or scooters. Manufacturers have responded to this demand by expanding production and developing more sophisticated models.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: These cars provide essential mobility for those without a full licence, including young people and those living in areas with limited public transport. While they offer independence, they are restricted to lower speeds and are forbidden on motorways. Some users express concerns regarding safety when sharing roads with faster traffic, describing the vehicles as vulnerable compared to larger cars and trucks.

sections.text: Leaked data from the Russian statistics agency Rosstat, analysed by the BBC, suggests that 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. gist: Hundreds complained about I'm A Celebrity after Mariella Frostrup called AJ Odudu aggressive.
Frostrup discussed gender double standards, whilst Odudu highlighted how language affects Black women.
ITV stated it monitors camp contestants constantly and takes duty of care seriously.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Hundreds of people complained about I'm A Celebrity after Mariella Frostrup called AJ Odudu aggressive. Frostrup argued that forthright women are often labelled aggressive, whereas forthright men are called strong. Odudu agreed with the point on gender but explained that the word carries extra weight when used in casual scenarios towards Black women. Friction resurfaced when Frostrup remarked that Odudu did not take an apology well.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The exchange highlighted sensitive conversations around race and gender-based language on television. ITV stated that production monitors camp members constantly, maintaining measures to protect contestant welfare and intervening if anyone uses inappropriate language or oversteps the line.

quotes.text: Well, I wasn't being aggressive, so it shouldn't have been there.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The BBC lodged an urgent appeal with a higher court following a federal judge's decision to permit a defamation lawsuit from Donald Trump to move forward. Trump filed the ten billion dollar suit regarding a Panorama documentary segment that edited his January 2021 speech before the US Capitol riot. The BBC previously apologised for the misleading edit but argued the case fails to meet defamation criteria and that the programme was never shown in Florida.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The corporation argues the Florida court has no jurisdiction, citing no evidence the documentary was accessed there and noting rigorous efforts to block US access. The legal battle presents significant time and financial costs for the BBC while it undergoes domestic budget cuts.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: A higher court will review the jurisdictional ruling. Meanwhile, Trump must answer questions under oath by January twenty-second, and a trial date is scheduled for May third, 2027, in Florida.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: US federal regulators approved SpaceX to deploy up to one million Starmind orbital satellites for space data centres. The approval marks the first authorization of its kind for space-based computing modules designed to harness solar power for artificial intelligence.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Terrestrial data centres face increasing public pushback, power grid strains, and water usage limits. Proponents argue space data centres offer an energy-efficient alternative, while critics highlight major engineering hurdles, collision risks, and space debris concerns.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Under the licence conditions, SpaceX must begin deploying the satellites no later than November 2033. The company must deploy 10 percent by November 2035 and 50 percent by November 2038, though critics question whether the full deployment is realistic.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A deadly fire tore through the eight-block Wang Fuk Court apartment complex in Hong Kong during mandated renovations on 26 November. The blaze killed 168 people, fueled by cheaper non-fire-retardant replacement netting, blocked fire escapes, and turned-off fire alarms.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A court in Düsseldorf granted Fender copyright protection for the Stratocaster design after a Chinese seller did not appear. Fender then launched a campaign sending cease and desist letters to retailers and manufacturers to stop making and selling Strat lookalikes in Europe. In response, German musical instrument retailer Thomann started legal action against Fender, and Fender subsequently sued Thomann for copyright infringement.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The dispute creates intense concern in the guitar world because the Stratocaster shape has been widely copied by countless manufacturers since the 1960s and is considered a generic design by many. While large companies like Thomann can afford to challenge Fender, smaller independent guitar builders lack the financial and legal resources to fight such legal demands.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Legal cases are continuing in Germany as Thomann seeks legal clarity for the wider guitar industry. Meanwhile, Fender stated it remains confident in the original Düsseldorf court judgement and is focusing more on targeting larger manufacturers while listening to smaller builders.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The government announced a shake-up of stalking laws following a review led by Richard Wright KC. Stalking will become a single standalone offence in England and Wales, removing the need to establish an underlying offence of harassment first. Ministers rejected a recommendation to raise the maximum sentence from 10 to 14 years, arguing existing maximums are not fully used.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Previous laws were described as cluttered and confused, which campaigners and victims said hindered prosecutions and placed too much onus on victims to prove fear or distress. While families of victims and campaigners welcomed the simplification, some expressed disappointment that maximum sentences were not increased and that certain recommendations were not fully adopted.

timeline.text: Has global jihadism failed, or is it simply changing shape?

gist: Jihadist groups are shifting from global attacks to local power struggles and tactical compromises.
Groups like JNIM and al-Shabab are adopting rebranding and alliance strategies.
Experts debate whether this pragmatism represents genuine moderation or a strategic Trojan horse.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Jihadist movements are changing shape a quarter of a century after the 9/11 attacks and 12 years after the Islamic State declared its caliphate. Rather than focusing solely on attacking the West or pursuing global jihad, groups like al-Qaeda's Sahel branch JNIM and Somali branch al-Shabab are focusing on local power. They are rebranding, providing aid, forming local alliances, and dropping familiar global jihadist slogans to win over local populations.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: This shift is inspired by the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan and Syria's president Ahmed al-Sharaa, who used pragmatism and local alliances to rise to power. A debate is growing within the jihadist movement between hardliners who reject compromise and pragmatists who see cooperation as a pathway to gaining control.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: It remains unclear whether pragmatic approaches will genuinely moderate these groups or serve as a Trojan horse strategy to secure power. Meanwhile, groups like the Islamic State reject compromise entirely and maintain global ambitions.

fivew: Jihadist groups including al-Shabab and JNIM.
Jihadist groups are shifting their tactics toward local power struggles and tactical compromises.
To win local support, build power bases, and adapt to changing geopolitical conditions.

timeline.text: DR Congo demands answers over Ugandan general's threats

gist: DR Congo summoned Uganda's diplomat over social media threats from a Ugandan general.
General Muhoozi Kainerugaba suggested a rebel takeover of a mineral-rich Congolese territory.
The Congolese government requested official clarification from Uganda regarding these provocative statements.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Democratic Republic of Congo summoned the Ugandan envoy following social media posts by General Muhoozi Kainerugaba. The general, who is the son of Uganda's president, appeared to endorse a rebel seizure of Walikale, a territory known for gold and tin. He also criticised the alleged presence of foreign mercenaries in the region.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The Congolese foreign ministry described the comments as highly serious and damaging to diplomatic ties. These remarks threaten the stability of the relationship between the two neighbours, who currently cooperate on joint military operations against the Allied Democratic Forces.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Congolese government expects Uganda to clarify its official stance and implement measures to stop such incidents. Meanwhile, the general's social media account has become inaccessible.

stories.title: Thirteen dead as mine disaster highlights illegal hunt for gold
stories.standfirst: Indonesian authorities say another 13 are missing in the illegal gold mine, which flooded on Monday.

articles.title: Thirteen dead as mine disaster highlights illegal hunt for gold
articles.standfirst: Indonesian authorities say another 13 are missing in the illegal gold mine, which flooded on Monday.

timeline.text: Thirteen dead as mine disaster highlights illegal hunt for gold

gist: Thirteen miners died after flooding at an illegal gold mine in Bogor, Indonesia.
Search and rescue efforts continue for at least thirteen people still missing underground.
Illegal mining remains widespread despite government bans and frequent, dangerous accidents.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Torrential rain caused a river to overflow, flooding two shafts at an illegal gold mine in Bogor, West Java. Thirteen people have been confirmed dead, while at least thirteen others remain missing. Rescue operations are ongoing, though personnel face significant challenges due to the depth, narrow access and limited lighting within the shafts.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The disaster highlights the dangers of Indonesia's widespread illegal gold mining industry. Experts suggest the sector is supported by corruption, with backers often including officials or security forces. While the mines provide economic opportunities, they lack regulation and safety standards, leading to frequent, often fatal, accidents.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Indonesian Ombudsman has called for a comprehensive investigation to address systemic issues. They urge authorities to target the networks and financiers behind illegal mining rather than only prosecuting individual miners. Meanwhile, search efforts continue as families wait for news of the missing.

fivew: Illegal gold miners were working in the pits when the disaster struck.
Thirteen people died and others are missing after an illegal gold mine flooded.
The flooding occurred on Monday night.
The incident took place in Bogor, West Java province, Indonesia.
Torrential rain caused a nearby river to overflow into the mine shafts.

As long as these backers are not dealt with firmly, illegal mining will continue.

stories.standfirst: Leaders of major Welsh powers reviews want to see the evidence behind Andy Burnham's stance.

articles.standfirst: Leaders of major Welsh powers reviews want to see the evidence behind Andy Burnham's stance.

timeline.text: Constitutional experts challenge PM's rejection of more Welsh powers

gist: Constitutional experts challenge the Prime Minister's refusal to grant Wales further devolved powers.
The Prime Minister rejected calls for control over policing, justice, and rail infrastructure.
Welsh political leaders expressed disappointment, claiming the Prime Minister does not treat Wales equally.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Prime Minister Andy Burnham rejected requests to transfer powers regarding policing, justice, the Crown Estate, and rail infrastructure to Wales. Four constitutional experts criticised this decision, stating that the Prime Minister failed to provide an evidence-based counter-argument. This follows previous discussions between the Prime Minister and First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The rejection has caused tension between the UK and Welsh governments. Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iorwerth expressed deep disappointment, suggesting the Prime Minister does not view Wales as an equal nation. While the Prime Minister maintains he is listening to Wales, he prefers to focus on devolving employment support where he identifies common ground.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Prime Minister stated he would never completely rule out future changes, though current efforts remain focused on areas of agreement such as employment support.

fivew: Prime Minister Andy Burnham and four constitutional experts.

timeline.text: Guinea orders residents to clean up the capital months after deadly rubbish dump collapse

gist: Guinea has ordered a mass clean-up of Conakry following a deadly landfill collapse.
The government set a 31 December deadline to clear rubbish from city streets.
Authorities plan to convert the closed Dar es Salaam dump into an urban park.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Following a fatal landslide at the Dar es Salaam rubbish dump in August, which killed 31 people, the site was permanently closed. This closure, combined with collection system weaknesses, has led to significant waste accumulation across Conakry. Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah has now mandated that the capital and its suburbs must be cleared of rubbish by 31 December.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The accumulation of waste poses ongoing sanitation challenges for the capital, which generates approximately 3,000 tonnes of garbage daily. The government aims to improve collection efficiency and create jobs through local municipal involvement and a new national sanitation fund.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The government is finalising plans to transport waste to a new disposal site in Baretodé. Additionally, officials intend to transform the site of the former landfill into an urban park.

gist: UK net migration has fallen to 77,000 in the year to June.
The drop is driven by fewer arrivals for work, study, and asylum.
Politicians from different parties dispute who deserves credit for the decrease.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: UK net migration fell to 77,000 in the year to June, down from 204,000 in the previous 12 months and a peak of 944,000 in 2023. This marks the lowest level since 1997 excluding the Covid pandemic. The decline was driven by drops in work visas, student arrivals, and asylum claims, following visa restrictions introduced by successive Conservative and Labour administrations.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The figures fulfill a long-standing target to bring net migration into the tens of thousands, first pledged by David Cameron in 2010. While politicians welcomed the drop, researchers warned that falls in skilled work visas could carry a fiscal cost, while reductions in asylum migration may benefit public finances.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Researchers suggest net migration may drop further next year. Meanwhile, political debate continues, with the Conservatives calling for a legally binding annual cap and Labour defending its current policies.

fivew: Reported by the Office for National Statistics and discussed by various UK politicians.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Anthony Williams carried out knife attacks in Peterborough and on a London railway before boarding an East Coast Mainline train. He stabbed ten people during a five-minute period near Huntingdon last November.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The attacks highlight potential missed chances by healthcare providers and police. Williams had contacted his doctor reporting that his psychosis drugs were not working, and authorities are now investigating previous police actions and his medical care.

sections.heading: What happens next

timeline.text: Water levels fell sharply in world’s rivers and lakes in two hottest years on record, study finds

gist: Extreme global heat caused unprecedented declines in global freshwater levels during 2023 and 2024.
Global river flows fell to 5.7% below normal while lake and reservoir storage dropped.
South America experienced particularly large decreases in river flows and surface water.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: An international study led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences found that surface freshwater fell sharply across the world in 2023 and 2024. Global river flows dropped by about 5.7% below normal, and water stored in lakes and reservoirs decreased by 9.5%.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The findings highlight that a warmer atmosphere does not mean more available water on land, as additional rainfall often occurs over oceans. The study shows how exposed global water supplies are to climate change and extreme weather.

fivew: An international study led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences
Global surface freshwater levels fell sharply in an unprecedented decline.
Extreme global heat and a more extreme water cycle caused by a warming atmosphere

quotes.text: The findings highlight an important paradox of climate change: a warmer atmosphere does not necessarily mean more water is available on land.
A river can flood during a downpour and still run low for much of the year.

gist: The inaugural Children's Booker prize announced its shortlist and child judges.
Child judges will help decide the winner alongside adult judges on the panel.
The winning book will be announced in February next year in London.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The first Children's Booker prize revealed its shortlist and the children chosen to judge the books. A panel of child judges, along with adults including Frank Cottrell-Boyce, Lolly Adefope and Sanchita Basu De Sarkar, will determine the winner. The announcement of the victorious book is scheduled for February next year at the Young V and A in London, accompanied by the distribution of 30,000 copies to children in need.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The prize aims to address concerning statistics regarding declining reading enjoyment among children and young people. By including children on the judging panel, the organisers ensure that young readers have a direct and powerful voice in deciding which book deserves to win.

gist: Sabrina Bahsoon experienced sudden psychotic symptoms initially misdiagnosed as stress and lack of sleep.
She was sectioned before doctors discovered she had anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis caused by ovarian tumours.
Bahsoon is now recovering in Malaysia and hopes to raise awareness of the rare disease.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Content creator Sabrina Bahsoon began experiencing erratic behaviour and psychotic symptoms in March. After being discharged from A&E with sleeping tablets, police brought her to hospital where she was sectioned and treated with antipsychotic medication. Two months later, she was diagnosed with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis caused by ovarian tumours, and had surgery in June.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Bahsoon wants to raise awareness of the rare autoimmune disease and encourage people to advocate for their treatment. An NHS trust apologised after an internal review found initial assessment aspects were not followed up properly.

fivew: Sabrina Bahsoon was misdiagnosed with psychosis before discovering she had anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
To raise awareness of the rare disease and encourage people to advocate for themselves.

sections.text: Mauricio Pochettino began his tenure as Manchester United manager with a 4-0 defeat at Liverpool. Leny Yoro was shown a red card after eight minutes, and United quickly conceded two goals.

sections.text: The heavy defeat leaves United 19th in the Premier League table after 11 games, highlighting the massive scale of the task facing Pochettino after leaving his United States job.
